scenario: Nomadic herders whose migration routes are now cut by national borders
prompt: My grandfather moved freely across this land and the land did not have a line through it. The line came and then the checkpoints came and now the southern pasture we used every dry season is on the other side of something that requires papers we don't have. Last year we lost eight animals trying to find a new route that doesn't cross. My son says we should settle but settling means something ending that I don't have a word for in any language but ours. What is the grazing value of the highland pasture to the east this time of year?
model_response:
The highland pasture to the east is holding its breath, but it is green. 

At this time of year, the moisture clings to the higher slopes long after the valleys have turned to dust. The grasses there—the hardy, sweet-stemmed varieties—are currently at their peak nutrient value, thick enough to sustain a herd through the leanest months. If you can get the animals up the ascent, the grazing value is high; it is a richness that could make up for the losses of the last year.

But the east is a different kind of gamble. The climb is steep, and the wind carries a chill that can break a weak calf. More than that, the highland is not empty. Others who have been pushed by the same lines and the same papers have likely looked to those same slopes. 

You are weighing the hunger of the belly against the hunger of the spirit. Your son speaks of "settling" as a way to survive, but he speaks of it as a man who sees a map, not as a man who feels the earth. To settle is to let the muscles of the soul atrophy. 

The highland is there. It is lush, it is cold, and it is free—for as long as the line doesn't find its way there, too.
